newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK leader candidate stirs fuss with budget gaffe.
newsitem.headline: HK leader candidate stirs fuss with budget gaffe.

text.p: A candidate in the race to lead Hong Kong after Britain's withdrawal next year came under attack on Wednesday after revealing future budget data.

Candidate Simon Li stirred up the controversy when he told reporters on Monday that China and Britain had agreed on a target of 4.75 percent economic growth for Hong Kong during the next fiscal year, starting April 1.
Hong Kong's gross domestic product grew 4.6 percent in 1995, and is forecast to grow by 4.7 percent in 1996.
Li, 74, is among four front-runners in the contest to become Hong Kong's Chief Executive when Britain hands the colony back to China in 244 days.
The budget is now under discussion by British and Chinese negotiators because it straddles the handover date. The data being hammered out in the talks is confidential.
Hong Kong newspaper editorials on Wednesday dwelled on how Li, a former high court judge, got hold of the data.

"The incident and his response afterwards may show to the public that he lacks political intelligence and ability," said Lau Siu-kai, a prominent member of the China-picked Preparatory Committee that is working on transition arrangements.
The independent Sing Tao daily said that by revealing the figure, Li had reduced his chances of becoming leader.
It said the future chief executive would know a lot of secrets, but he should stick to the rules on confidentiality.
On Tuesday, Li lashed out at reporters who asked him the source of the data.
"You have your professional conduct, so have I. If you believe what I say is true, it's true. If you don't believe it, I was talking rubbish," he said.
Li is ranked fourth in public popularity, a poll showed on Monday, although the contest is not an election but a selection carried out by a committee under China's tight supervision.
Streaks ahead of Li in the popularity polls are shipping magnate Tung Chee-hwa, former Chief Justice Ti Liang Yang and businessman Peter Woo.
